plan.title: Sound & Music: Waves, Pitch & Resonance
plan.hook: A note on a piano is three separate facts wearing one name: how high it is, how loud it is, and why it sounds like a piano at all. This course separates them — and shows why the air carrying the note never actually goes anywhere.
objectives: Explain how a longitudinal pressure wave travels while air particles only oscillate in place, using frequency × wavelength = wave speed
Separate pitch, loudness, and timbre by what each one tracks: fundamental frequency, amplitude, and spectrum shape with envelope
Describe a standing wave on a string fixed at both ends — nodes at the ends — and give the fundamental frequency as wave speed over twice the length

sections.heading: The pattern travels; air oscillates locally
points: Ordinary sound in air is a longitudinal pressure wave
Air particles oscillate around their own positions; the pattern travels, the air stays nearby
Frequency times wavelength equals wave speed

sections.heading: Three different questions about a note
points: Pitch tracks fundamental frequency; loudness tracks amplitude
Timbre tracks spectrum shape and envelope
The same pitch can still sound different — three questions about a note have three different answers

sections.heading: Boundaries select a standing pattern
points: For a string fixed at both ends, the ends are nodes
Nodes stay still; antinodes move most
Fundamental frequency is wave speed over twice the length

questions.q: A speaker plays a steady tone across the room. Does the air next to the speaker end up next to you?
questions.hint: Follow one particle, as the visual suggests.
questions.answer: No. Air particles oscillate around their own positions; the pattern travels, but the air itself stays nearby. Sound in air is a longitudinal pressure wave.

questions.q: How are frequency, wavelength, and wave speed related?
questions.hint: The body states it as a single multiplication.
questions.answer: Frequency times wavelength equals wave speed. Double the frequency at the same speed and the wavelength halves.

sections.heading: Three different questions about a note
sections.body: Pitch tracks fundamental frequency. Loudness tracks amplitude. Timbre tracks spectrum shape and envelope.
sections.visual: Pitch, amplitude and timbre answer different questions about the same note. Harmonic bars show spectral shape.

questions.q: Two instruments play the same note at the same volume, yet sound different. Which property explains it?
questions.hint: Run through the three questions: pitch, loudness, and...?
questions.answer: Timbre. Pitch tracks fundamental frequency and loudness tracks amplitude — both are matched here — while timbre tracks spectrum shape and envelope, which differ between instruments.

questions.q: What does loudness track, if not frequency?
questions.hint: The diagram assigns one quantity to each of the three questions.
questions.answer: Amplitude. Pitch tracks fundamental frequency, loudness tracks amplitude, and timbre tracks spectrum shape and envelope.

sections.heading: Boundaries select a standing pattern
sections.body: For a string fixed at both ends, ends are nodes. Fundamental frequency is wave speed over twice the length.
sections.visual: Nodes stay still; antinodes move most. Scrub through the standing-wave cycle.

questions.q: On a string fixed at both ends, what happens at the ends themselves?
questions.hint: The ends have a special name in the standing pattern.
questions.answer: They are nodes: points that stay still. Between them, antinodes are where the string moves most.

questions.q: What sets the fundamental frequency of a fixed-end string?
questions.hint: It is a ratio of wave speed to a length, from the body.
questions.answer: The fundamental frequency is wave speed over twice the length: f = v / 2L. A longer string means a lower fundamental.

questions.q: In a longitudinal sound wave, an individual air particle…
choices: Travels with the wave from speaker to listener
Oscillates around its own position while the pattern travels
Moves only when the sound is loud
Stays perfectly still — only pressure moves
questions.explain: The visual follows one particle: it does not travel across the diagram. Air oscillates locally; what crosses the room is the pattern of the longitudinal pressure wave.

questions.q: A wave has frequency 100 Hz and wavelength 3.4 m. Its speed is…
questions.explain: Frequency times wavelength equals wave speed: 100 × 3.4 = 340 m/s.

questions.q: Pitch, loudness, and timbre track, in order…
choices: Fundamental frequency, amplitude, spectrum shape and envelope
questions.explain: The diagram assigns one quantity to each question: pitch → fundamental frequency, loudness → amplitude, timbre → spectrum shape (and envelope).

questions.q: The same pitch can still sound different because…
choices: Timbre depends on spectrum shape and envelope, which vary by source
Each note has a unique wavelength
questions.explain: Pitch only fixes the fundamental frequency. Two sources can share it while their harmonic spectrum and envelope — timbre — differ, so the notes sound different.

questions.q: For a string fixed at both ends, the ends are…
choices: Free to move like the middle
Where the wave reflects silently without a pattern
questions.explain: Boundaries select the standing pattern: the fixed ends are nodes that stay still, and antinodes between them move most.

questions.q: A string sounds its fundamental at 110 Hz. If the wave speed on the string stays the same but the string is made twice as long, the new fundamental is…
questions.explain: Fundamental frequency is wave speed over twice the length, f = v / 2L. Doubling the length halves the frequency: 110 / 2 = 55 Hz.

sections.title: The wave travels; the air stays
bullets: Sound in air is a longitudinal pressure wave.
Air particles oscillate around their own positions.
The pattern crosses the room; the air does not.
sections.notes: Follow one air particle and the illusion breaks: it jiggles in place while the disturbance hands itself along. What reaches the listener is a pattern, not a parcel of air.
sections.visual: The speaker moves back and forth. Air particles oscillate around their own positions. Follow one particle: it does not travel across the diagram.

sections.title: Three questions about one note
bullets: Same pitch can still sound different.
sections.notes: One note, three independent facts. Keep the questions separate and the vocabulary stops tangling: frequency questions, amplitude questions, and spectrum questions have different answers.
sections.visual: Pitch, amplitude and timbre answer different questions about the same note. Harmonic bars show spectral shape.

sections.title: Boundaries pick the pattern
bullets: A string fixed at both ends has nodes at the ends.
Nodes stay still; antinodes move most.
sections.notes: Pin both ends and only certain patterns fit. The simplest — one hump between two still ends — is the fundamental, and its frequency falls straight out of the wave speed and the length.
sections.visual: Nodes stay still; antinodes move most. Scrub through the standing-wave cycle.

enrichment.audioTitle: Sound & Music: Waves, Pitch & Resonance — a conversation

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: A tone plays across the room. A speck of dust hangs in the air near the speaker. By the time the sound reaches you, where is the speck?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: That is the picture to unlearn. Air particles oscillate around their own positions — the speck jiggles in place. What crosses the room is the pattern of a longitudinal pressure wave.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: So frequency times wavelength equals the speed of that pattern.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Exactly. Now take one note from two instruments, same pitch, same volume. Why do they sound different?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Different... pitch quality? They have the same pitch, so something else.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Run the three questions. Pitch tracks what?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Fundamental frequency. Loudness tracks amplitude. So the difference must be timbre — spectrum shape and envelope.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Right — the harmonic bars differ even when the fundamental matches. Last idea: a string fixed at both ends. What is special about the ends?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: They cannot move — they are nodes. The middle moves most at the antinodes.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: And the fundamental frequency of that string?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Wave speed over twice the length. Longer string, lower note.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Then halving the string's length should double the fundamental, from that same formula.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: It follows directly: f = v / 2L, so half the length at the same wave speed gives twice the frequency. That is why the short strings are the high ones.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Which ties the course shut: waves carry patterns, notes answer three separate questions, and boundaries choose which patterns may stand.
